SOURCE: "A Survey on Agent-as-a-Judge". Runyang You*, Hongru Cai*, Caiqi Zhang, Qiancheng Xu, Meng Liu, Tiezheng Yu, Yongqi Li† (corresponding), Wenjie Li (* equal contribution). Affiliations as printed: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, University of Cambridge, Shandong Jianzhu University, Huawei Technologies. Printed on the PDF: "arXiv:2601.05111v1 [cs.CL] 8 Jan 2026". No venue is printed, so treat it as a preprint (the Ethics Statement mentions "the conference" without naming one). It is a survey and reports no experiments of its own.

COVERAGE: 15 of 15 pages, 64,830 of 64,830 chars. Body is pp. 1-10, Limitations and Ethics are on p. 11, references [1]-[66] run pp. 11-15 and were read for origins. There is no appendix.

File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/you-2026-agent-as-judge.pdf

CLAIMS

There are no quantitative results anywhere in the paper: no agreement rates, cost multiples, latency figures or benchmark scores. Every claim below is qualitative, so `number` is "none" throughout. Any number a note attaches to this source would be unsupported.

- claim: Single-pass LLM judges have three weaknesses: parametric bias (verbosity, own-output patterns), no verification against the world, and overload on multi-dimension rubrics that produces coarse scores.
  number: none
  setup: framing argument, backed by citations [7], [8], [9] rather than measurement
  quote: "single-pass evaluators are prone to inherent parametric biases—such as favoring verbosity or their own output patterns"
  where: p. 1
- claim: Static judges grade plausibility, not correctness; agentic judges replace this with execution (query system state, run code or theorem provers, search).
  number: none
  setup: conceptual; examples cited are [48], [51], [37], [38], [8]
  quote: "They assess answers based on linguistic plausibility – how correct a response looks – without verification or evidence collection, leading to "hallucinated correctness" in complex tasks [8]."
  where: p. 3
- claim: Agentic judges fall into three stages: Procedural (fixed workflows or fixed-role debate), Reactive (routing and tool calls driven by intermediate feedback) and Self-Evolving (rubrics and memory refined during operation).
  number: none
  setup: the authors' own taxonomy, sec. 2.3
  quote: "such reactivity remains confined to conditional routing within fixed decision spaces, lacking autonomy to refine underlying rubrics"
  where: p. 4
- claim: Methods are organised on five dimensions: multi-agent collaboration, planning, tool integration, memory and personalization, optimization paradigms.
  number: none
  setup: sec. 3; multi-agent splits into Collective Consensus (debate, e.g. ChatEval) and Task Decomposition (e.g. HiMATE, SAGEval "Judge the Judge" meta-evaluator)
  quote: "Multi-agent evaluation frameworks adopt two main topologies: Collective Consensus and Task Decomposition."
  where: p. 5
- claim: Tool use serves two purposes: evidence collection and correctness verification (Table 1 lists seven methods with task and tool types).
  number: none
  setup: Table 1, p. 6
  quote: "Agent-as-a-Judge [48] records execution traces and step-level feedback, enabling evaluation beyond final outputs to account for intermediate behavior."
  where: p. 6 (relevant to outcome versus trajectory grading in note 06)
- claim: Agentic judging costs more per evaluation and is slower, which can rule it out under latency budgets; it also widens the attack surface and can amplify judge bias when used as a reward signal.
  number: none
  setup: sec. 5.1, asserted without measurement
  quote: "Unlike single-pass judgment, agentic evaluation typically involves multiple reasoning steps, intermediate decisions, and coordination among multiple agents, all of which increase computation per evaluation."
  where: p. 9
- claim: Planning can discover rubrics as well as order the workflow; OnlineRubrics evolves rubrics during RL to detect reward hacking.
  number: none
  setup: sec. 3.2, descriptions of cited systems
  quote: "enabling agents to optimize how they evaluate (workflow orchestration) and what they evaluate (rubric discovery)"
  where: p. 5 (spaces restored; the extraction runs words together)

LIMITS
- Conceded by the authors (p. 11): no consensus definition of an evaluation agent; many included "agent" systems are prompt engineering with fixed role-play. Quote: "Many pioneering works in automated evaluation, though named as "agent", rely heavily on prompting engineering, such as fixed role-play".
- Not shown: no evidence that agentic judges agree with humans more than single-pass judges. "More robust, verifiable, and nuanced" is asserted from cited papers, with no numbers reproduced and no head-to-head comparison.
- Cost and latency are named but never quantified.
- No inclusion criteria, search method or paper count is stated. Coverage is mostly 2024-2025 work, much of it arXiv-only.
- No discussion of how to validate an agentic judge itself (meta-evaluation), beyond naming SAGEval's meta-judge.
- Bias reduction through debate is claimed, but conformity to the majority is acknowledged only in passing (p. 4, citing [64]).
- Self-preference bias is attributed to [7] (Wang et al., "Large language models are not fair evaluators", ACL 2024). I did not read [7], so check it before citing it for that specific bias.

BUILDS ON
- Origin of the name: Zhuge et al., "Agent-as-a-judge: Evaluate agents with agents", Forty-second International Conference on Machine Learning, 2025 (ref [48]). The survey cites it as one method (code generation; graph/locate/read/search/retrieve tools) and does not explicitly credit it as the origin of the term.
- LLM-as-a-judge: Zheng et al., MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, NeurIPS 2023 [1]; G-Eval, Liu et al., EMNLP 2023 [59]; Prometheus, Kim et al., ICLR [60]; JudgeLM, Zhu et al., ICLR 2025 [61].
- Multi-agent debate judging: ChatEval, Chan et al., ICLR 2024 [10].
- Tool-verified reward: Agentic Reward Modeling, Peng et al., ACL 2025 [8].
- Prior survey: Li et al., "From generation to judgment", EMNLP 2025 [2].

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- One candidate: Figure 1, p. 2, "Comparison between LLM-as-a-Judge (1a) and Agent-as-a-Judge (1b). The former performs direct single-pass evaluation, while the latter leverages planning, memory, and tool-augmented capabilities for enhanced evaluation." It shows the two judge shapes side by side, which fits the judge-shapes section of note 05.
- Table 1 (p. 6) is the more information-dense alternative if a table is preferred over a schematic. Figure 2 (taxonomy, p. 3) is a list of system names and reads poorly as a slide.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the PDF.
- Extraction frequently drops spaces ("LLM-as-a-Judgehas", "parametricbiases—suchasfavoringverbosity"); quotes above are copied from the extraction except where I flagged restored spaces.
- Inconsistencies in the source itself: "NarrativeFactScore" in Figure 2 versus "NarrativeFastScore" in the text (p. 8); GEMA-Score is cited as "[24, 58]" on p. 4 although [58] is CourtEval; ref [19] has a malformed markdown-style URL.
- Figure text (Figs 1, 3, 4) extracted only as loose labels; I did not view the images.
